This page runs R inside your browser. It needs about 20 MB on first load — the

`tibble()` in Primer 2 was not part of base R. It arrived in a **package**, and
a package's functions are out of reach until you ask for them. This page covers
the two lines of plumbing that every tidyverse script needs: `library()`, which
puts a package's functions within reach, and `|>`, which chains those functions
together in the order you think about them. For the full explanation, see
[the R primer](r-primer.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning title="One way this browser lies to you"}
This page has already loaded `dplyr` for you before you ran anything. Your own
RStudio will not. There, every script starts with its `library()` calls, and a
script that forgets them fails with `could not find function`.

So the `library(dplyr)` line below is a no-op here and essential there. Type it
anyway — it is the habit that matters.
:::

## Packages

A package is a bundle of functions somebody else wrote and shared. You install
it **once, ever**, and load it **every session**.

```r
install.packages("dplyr")   # once, ever — in the console
library(dplyr)              # every session, at the top of every script
```

`library()` takes the package name without quotation marks. Run it, then use a
function that only exists because of it:

```{webr}
library(dplyr)

n_distinct(c("MBBS", "MBBS", "MD", "MD", "MD"))
```

`n_distinct()` counts distinct values: five enrolments there, but only `2`
distinct qualifications. It comes from dplyr, not from base R. Without
`library(dplyr)` in your own RStudio, that line stops with `could not find
function "n_distinct"` — the single most common error a beginner meets.

::: {.callout-warning title="`install.packages()` does not belong in your script"}
Put `library()` calls at the top of a script; keep `install.packages()` in the
console. A script that reinstalls its packages on every run is slow, needs an
internet connection it should not need, and is rude to whoever else runs it.
:::

## The native pipe `|>`

The pipe passes the thing on its left into the function on its right as that
function's first argument. These two lines do exactly the same thing:

```{webr}
round(mean(c(72, 68, 81, 90)), 1)

c(72, 68, 81, 90) |> mean() |> round(1)
```

Both print `77.8`. The first has to be read from the inside out: find the
innermost bracket, work outwards, and keep track of which closing bracket
belongs to what. The second reads left to right, in the order the work actually
happens — *take these scores, take the mean, round to one decimal*. Once an
analysis is six steps long, the pipe is the difference between readable and
unreadable code.

You will meet `%>%` in older code and in most tutorials online. For everything
in this workshop it behaves the same way, but we use `|>` because it is built
into R itself and needs no package.

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: unpick the nesting"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Four stations were marked out of 100: 16, 25, 36 and 49. Somebody has written
their root-mean score inside out. Rewrite it using `|>` so that it reads left
to right: take the vector, take its `mean()`, take the `sqrt()` of that, then
`round()` to 2 decimal places. The answer is `5.61` either way.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pipe
# The nested version, for reference:
# round(sqrt(mean(c(16, 25, 36, 49))), 2)

c(16, 25, 36, 49) ______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pipe
#| solution: true
c(16, 25, 36, 49) |> mean() |> sqrt() |> round(2)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pipe
#| check: true
# The only check in these primers that reads your code rather than your answer:
# the pipe is the lesson here, and the value 5.61 alone cannot prove you used it.
used_pipe <- grepl("|>", .user_code, fixed = TRUE)
right_answer <- isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 5.61))
if (right_answer && used_pipe) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — and it reads left to right.")
} else if (grepl("%>%", .user_code, fixed = TRUE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use the native pipe |>, not %>%. We use |> throughout this workshop.")
} else if (right_answer) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right answer, but rewrite it with |> so it reads in the order the work happens.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Start with the vector, then pipe into mean(), then sqrt(), then round(2).")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_pipe"}
Each step is one `|>` followed by a function with its brackets: `mean()`,
then `sqrt()`, then `round(2)`. The piped value fills the first argument, so
`round(2)` sets only the digits.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: mean attendance, piped"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Four students attended 88%, 72%, 95% and 64% of sessions. Starting from that
vector, pipe it into `mean()` and then into `round(1)` to get the mean
attendance to one decimal place.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pipe_mean
c(88, 72, 95, 64) ______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pipe_mean
#| solution: true
c(88, 72, 95, 64) |> mean() |> round(1)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pipe_mean
#| check: true
answer <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.result))
if (length(answer) == 1 && isTRUE(all.equal(answer, 79.8))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — mean attendance is 79.8%.")
} else if (length(answer) != 1 || is.na(answer)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is not a single number yet. Pipe the vector into mean() first.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(answer, 79.75))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the mean, unrounded. Pipe it on into round(1).")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(answer, 319))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the total of the four values. Use mean(), not sum().")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Two steps: |> mean() to average the vector, then |> round(1).")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_pipe_mean"}
The same shape as Exercise 1, one step shorter. `round(1)` means one decimal
place — the piped value is already the first argument.
:::
:::
